status: APPROVED BY THE OWNER, 2026-11-13, as part of the placement criteria set drafted by Task 7 of docs/superpowers/plans/2026-11-12-agent-pcb-place-and-route-phase-1.md and independently reviewed before it reached him. He was put the one deliberate judgement in the set - the extent of U1's zone in floorplan-intent.json - and ruled "loosen to 80%. The chip should be near the middle of the drawing, but perfect alignment is not critical". Nothing in THIS file changed under that ruling; it is approved as reviewed. READ `what_this_policy_does_not_do` BEFORE RELYING ON ANYTHING HERE: nothing in this file is enforced by code in Phase 1, so approval of it is not a claim that anything checks it. Changing it now invalidates every run made under it.
principle: An override is allowed only where this file lists it for that operation. Anything not listed is REFUSED, not defaulted and not quietly passed through. The reason is that every flag below changes what a run is graded against or what fabrication floor it is built to, so a flag nobody approved is a criterion nobody approved.
entry_points: The argv for each operation is the one Task 4's preflight recorded in build/krt/invocations.json, not a command invented at the point of use. This file names flags; it does not restate those invocations.

required.flag: the approved intent as the second argument
required.reason: The approved file declares no board coordinates: its geometry is fractions of whatever outline Task 8 settles on, and this step turns those into the rects and the compass edge the engine reads. Resolving a resolved file would double-apply the fractions, so the tool refuses an intent that already carries a rect or an edge.

forbidden.flag: editing the resolved file by hand
forbidden.reason: It is a derived artifact and belongs in a run directory under build/. A hand edit there is a coordinate nobody approved, in a file that looks machine-made.

post_conditions.check: Every later step in the run - seeding, refinement and grading - reads the SAME resolved file.
post_conditions.why: Two resolutions of one intent against two outlines are two different criteria. A run that seeds against one and grades against another reports a verdict about neither.

resolve-intent.note: The tool refuses a board with no Edge.Cuts rather than defaulting a rectangle, because the outline is Task 8's decision and a rectangle invented at this step would become the design by accident.

required.reason: The grader's long-standing default is that an intent running ZERO rules exits 0. That is how a vacuous intent can constrain a placement with nothing while every consumer stays silent. Passing it is what makes 'graded clean' mean something, and it is required on every invocation, not merely allowed.

required.value: the run's own resolved-intent.json, produced by `resolve-intent` from the approved circuits/pt2399-core/floorplan-intent.json and this run's board
required.reason: The approved intent is the only thing this board is graded against, and the resolved copy is that intent with its fractions turned into this outline's rects - nothing else added. A run against any other file is not a run on this board, and a run manifest therefore hashes both files, not one.

allowed.reason: Writes every measurement to a file, which is what the run record keeps. Reporting only.
Suppresses the text report and keeps the machine summary. Reporting only; it cannot change a verdict.
Adds the advisory routability signals. They say the floorplan will fight the router, not that it breaks the intent, and they gate nothing.

forbidden.reason: It writes a starter intent READ OFF the board and grades clean by construction. Using it on this board would make the layout author the criteria it is then checked against - the exact failure this repository's standing invariant names. The approved intent was authored from the circuit model and nothing may regenerate it from a placement.
A modifier of --emit-intent, which is forbidden above.
Reports violations and exits 0 anyway. A skipped or failed check must never look like a passing one.

Grades the legality model at a clearance other than the board's own. Tighter manufactures violations that are not there; looser hides ones that are. The board's Default netclass is the right source and the tool already reads it.
Same objection as --clearance, for the outline gate. The board's own min_copper_edge_clearance comes from docs/standards/pcbway-fab-rules.md and is the figure to grade at.

Not needed and not approved. Every block in the approved intent is declared by `refs`, so no block derives its membership from the board. Permitting a derivation source would let block membership come from the layout rather than from the circuit model.

place.entry_point: py_placer/place_seed.py for the FIRST pass; py_placer/place_optimize.py only to refine a pass that already graded clean. Both are recorded in build/krt/invocations.json; neither is a command invented here.
place.the_two_contracts_are_opposite: `place_seed.py <in> <out> --intent <json>` seeds an INITIAL placement from the intent. `place_optimize.py <in> <out>` REFINES an existing one within a displacement cap. Confusing them is the hazard this entry exists to prevent - see first_placement_warning.

seeding_exit_codes.0: seeded and graded clean against the intent
seeding_exit_codes.3: cannot seed: the board has no Edge.Cuts outline, or it already looks placed
seeding_exit_codes.4: a board was written, but a part is unseated or the grade found errors

required.reason: The seeder is the one tool that reads the intent as a CONSTRAINT SOURCE rather than only as a gate, and the zone and the compass edge it reads exist only in the resolved copy. Seeded against the approved file alone it places no block early, its decap stage seats nothing, and the one enforced rule in the intent becomes unreachable - measured, zero clean seeds in sixteen runs.

allowed.reason: Chooses the packing order and jitter; the same seed reproduces byte for byte. It selects a candidate, not a criterion, and the pipeline's shape is a portfolio of seeds whose failures are discarded.

allowed.value: on the first pass only, and only to discard the update tool's scaffolding
allowed.reason: Without it the seeder refuses a board that already looks placed (exit 3). `--force` DISCARDS that placement rather than refining it, which is exactly what should happen to a mechanical grid nobody designed. Passing it to preserve a placement is a misreading: it destroys one.

Reorders the connectivity-centroid stage to seed large parts first. It changes which candidate comes out, not what is acceptable. Measured on this board's intent it made the grade worse, not better, so it is allowed and not recommended.
Emits the raw packed seed. Useful for attributing a failure to the packer rather than the polish; it cannot loosen a gate.

Moves only the parts violating the intent, worst first, each seated nearest its current pose. It is driven BY the criteria and cannot change them. Measured once on this board: it reported `1 repaired (0 moved)` and the grade still failed, so a repair that claims success is not evidence that one happened - read the regrade, not the repair line.

allowed.value: on a REFINEMENT run, whose input is a placement that has already graded clean against the resolved intent
allowed.reason: It bounds how far a part may move from where it already is. On a refinement that is a useful brake. On a first pass it is the trap below.

forbidden.value: on the first placement pass, or any run whose input is the board as the headless update tool left it

forbidden.reason: Same objection as on check-intent: seeding at a clearance other than the board's own produces a placement that is legal against nothing the board declares.

place.first_placement_warning: THE 24 FOOTPRINTS ON THIS BOARD SIT ON A MECHANICAL 15 mm GRID WRITTEN BY THE UPDATE TOOL. That is scaffolding so the parts exist somewhere; nobody designed it and it carries no intent. `place_optimize.py --max-displacement 3` refines an existing placement within 3 mm of where it already is, so running it on this board as it stands would return a tidied version of that grid - and the grid would then BE the floorplan, chosen by a tool and graded against an intent that had nothing to say about it. The first pass is therefore `place_seed.py`, which seeds from the intent instead. THE TOOL ALSO FORECLOSES THE HAZARD BETTER THAN THIS FILE DOES, which is worth knowing because nothing enforces this file in Phase 1: the seeder refuses a board that already looks placed at exit 3, and `--force` discards that placement rather than refining it. There is no path through `place_seed.py` by which an existing arrangement survives into the result. Task 4's preflight probed only the optimiser; the seeding entry point was found by this plan's independent reviewer, and build/krt/invocations.json now records BOTH its arms - the exit-3 refusal and the forced seed - because the refusal is the half that matters here.
place.note: Nothing in this operation writes the committed board. The spec's `adopt` is the only verb that does, and it is Phase 2.

required.reason: NOT OPTIONAL, and this is the standing route entry the plan calls for. The router's own fabrication tiers come from a different vendor's capability page and are looser than this project's standard in every dimension that matters; left to itself it necks a blocked track and shrinks a via DOWN that ladder, and will escalate tiers on its own. Supplying this file replaces those values with the standard's and collapses the ladder to a single hard rung, which also disables escalation. KiCad's DRC would catch the result afterwards; the router should not produce it in the first place.

allowed.reason: Selects which nets to route. It chooses work, not fabrication limits or acceptance criteria.
The run's own output path. The committed board is never the output of a route run.

forbidden.reason: It is the routing engine's tighter, more costly tier, taken from another vendor's page. This board's floor is docs/standards/pcbway-fab-rules.md and it reaches the router through --fab-overrides and nothing else. A rule tighter than the standard raises the price of every order.

post_conditions.check: The route run's output must not report FAB FLOOR RELAXED.
post_conditions.why: Task 4's preflight recorded that routing writes or modifies a .kicad_pro beside its output and MAY RELAX THE DRC FLOORS, printing that phrase when it does. A relaxed project file would make a later DRC pass against looser constraints than the standard, which is a false green with the evidence sitting in the run log. The run fails on the phrase; the board is not the thing being inspected here, the log is.

post_conditions.check: The .kicad_pro the run leaves beside its output must still satisfy tools/pcb/fab-standard.ts.
post_conditions.why: Same hazard, checked on the artifact rather than on the log, because a log line can be absent for reasons other than the floors being intact.

zone-refill.entry_point: py_router/route_planes.py creates the pour; kicad-cli fills it

required.value: both, on the kicad-cli drc invocation
required.reason: The pour does not exist as copper until it is filled, and the board that would be adopted and plotted is the SAVED post-refill one. --save-board is rejected without --refill-zones on the pinned KiCad, so the pair is the mechanism and not two choices.

allowed.reason: Which layers carry a pour. A geometry choice recorded in the run, not a criterion.
Which net the pour belongs to - GND on this board.

post_conditions.check: Same two FAB FLOOR RELAXED checks as `route`.
post_conditions.why: Task 4's preflight recorded the same side effect for route_planes.py.

custom_design_rules.why: Task 7 Step 3 asked whether the input and output proximity on J1 needs a .kicad_dru isolation rule. It does not, and the reasoning is a measurement rather than a shrug: it is recorded in circuits/pt2399-core/placement-rules.json under separation.input_to_output.kicad_dru_decision, and the two figures it turns on are re-derived by tests/pcb/placement-intent-geometry.test.ts on every run.
custom_design_rules.if_this_changes: A .kicad_dru is a graded input like the intent, the rules and this policy. Adding one later invalidates every run made before it, and it is approved the same way.

what_this_policy_does_not_do: Nothing here is enforced by code yet. The spec puts the refusing wrapper in Phase 2, and Phase 1 is the probe that decides whether there is a Phase 2. Until then this file is the list a reviewer and the owner hold a run against by reading it, and a run that used a flag not listed here is out of policy whether or not anything stopped it. It must not be read as a gate.
